cover.title: The [[journal|journal]]
cover.lead: The journal is the local disk where every write lands first. This deck explains how it works, and why it answers “[[missing]]” instead of returning zeros.
cover.notes: Source: docs/internals/rfcs/rfc-1-journal.md, commit a34d0b8. The RFC specifies behaviour, not the current code. Its on-disk format and its recovery after a crash are RFC 28, not covered here. Keys: → next, S speaker notes, ? help. Click any underlined term for its definition.

intro.two: The [[journal]] is the fast local disk that every write lands on and is acknowledged from, appending each write as a [[record]] at the end of a [[segment]] file, keeping it through a crash and serving reads of the bytes it still holds. It knows nothing about [[chunk|chunks]] or the bucket, because the [[engine]] does the uploading and then [[report|reports]] which bytes are [[offload|offloaded]], and only those bytes may be dropped to make room.
intro.twoNotes: From 'Start here · In plain words' and §1 Purpose. The journal answers exactly one question: do I hold these bytes, at what offset, and which version of them?
intro.knownLead: These terms come from RFC 0's glossary and from the RFCs this one builds on (2, 3, 6 and 8). Click one to see its definition.
intro.knownNotes: Every definition restates RFC 0's glossary row, which is the definition of record.
intro.newNotes: From 'Start here · The words you need', plus missing (§3.2), change version (§3.2, §3.4), removal marker (§3.6), placement index (§4), headroom (§6), unreclaimed bytes (§3.5, §7.1) and loss event (§3.8). The glossary at the end adds append stream, share tag and sequence number.
intro.clashNotes: Record: RFC 0's glossary has two rows, journal and metadata. Offload: RFC 0's verb table says it is not a client's flush. Sync: RFC 0 calls offloaded content 'synced to the remote tier'. Release: RFC 0 lists the journal sense and RFC 7's file sense. Durable: RFC 0 separates it from RFC 14's durable open. Handle: RFC 1 §3's Handle is a share's access to the journal.

problem.title: One overwrite during an upload
problem.notes: 'Start here · The problem, in one example', steps 1–4, and §3.3's example. Segment size and versions are the RFC's own example values. After step 5 a release of v42 is refused until an offer has carried it.

items: An acknowledged write survives the process dying from the moment it is acknowledged. It also survives a host crash or a power loss once it is [[sync|synced]], which happens when the client flushes or, at the latest, after a fixed time bound such as 1 s.
A read never returns zeros for bytes the [[journal|journal]] does not hold. It lists exactly those ranges as [[missing]] and leaves the caller's buffer untouched for them.
The journal never releases bytes the engine has not reported as [[offload|offloaded]]. A [[release]] that asks for any such bytes is refused as a whole, and nothing is released.
promises.footer: After a crash, the journal rebuilds what it held from its own files on the local disk. This step, run when the journal opens again, is called recovery. It checks the files against a few facts the engine keeps for the journal, such as how far the writes had been synced.
promises.notes: 'Start here · What this RFC promises', which cites §3.1, §3.2, §3.4, §3.5, §3.6, §5.2, §6 and RFC 28 §3. The fifth promise is about writes; removals and releases draw on reserved space instead (§6). The 1 s bound is a proposal (§5.2, 'proposal: 1 s'); the slide gives it as an example.
promises.notes2: Deck framing: the fill and limit promises of 'Start here · What this RFC promises' (§3.4, §6). The fifth promise is about writes; removals and releases draw on reserved space instead (§6). The footer: 'Start here · What this RFC promises' (the journal rebuilds itself from its own files alone) and §4 (the placement index is built at recovery). How recovery reads the files is RFC 28 §3, which this deck does not cover. Recovery checks the files against what the caller passes to Open (§3): the version floor, and per stream the sync mark of its last recorded sync, against which a lost synced tail is detected (RFC 28 §3.3).
items2: A [[fill]], which puts bytes fetched from the bucket back, never overwrites bytes the journal holds. It is refused if the file changed after the read that found the bytes missing.
A write that would go over a limit is refused at once, with an error that names the limit. It never waits for space and never goes over.

notebook.title: A notebook you only write at the end of
notebook.analogy: Every write is added at the end of the notebook, and the client gets its answer from there. Later the [[engine|engine]] copies those bytes to the bucket and says which of them arrived. Only those may be thrown away to make room.
notebook.stops: You cannot tear out one page. Space comes back only when a whole notebook — one [[segment]] file — is thrown away, after its live pages are copied into a newer one.
notebook.missing: When it is asked for bytes it no longer has, the [[journal|journal]] answers “[[missing]]”. It never hands back blank zeros in their place.
notebook.notes: The analogy and its limit are the RFC's own: 'Start here · In plain words'. The rule behind the limit: §2 and §7.1, storage is freed in whole segments only.

extents.title: [[held-extent|Held extents]], by example
extents.notes: §2, 'What an extent is, by example'. An extent says which bytes of the file, never where on disk nor what content. Held extents are disjoint, need not be adjacent, and need not start at zero. One record can end up as several held extents, or none.

gaps.title: The journal cannot explain a gap
gaps.lead: A gap can have three causes, but the [[journal|journal]] sees the same thing in all three: it does not hold the bytes.
gaps.c1: The range is a [[hole]] that was never written. Only the metadata knows that it reads as zeros.
gaps.c2: The bytes were [[offload|offloaded]] to the bucket, then [[release|released]] from the journal to make room.
gaps.c3: The bytes were written, but they have been lost since.
gaps.rule: The journal reports all three in the same way, as [[missing]], and leaves the caller's buffer untouched. Telling them apart is the [[engine]]'s job.
gaps.exact: The `missing` list is exact. It is never widened to a whole [[segment|segment]], [[record|record]] or [[block|block]], because the caller pays for a remote transfer for every entry in it. Zeros would be worse: if the file is a virtual disk that Windows mounts, such as a profile kept in a `.vhdx` file, they would hand Windows a corrupt disk that looks valid.
gaps.notes: §2 (the gaps carry no explanation), §3.2 (ReadAt), §1.1 (non-goals). The Windows remark is from 'Start here · The problem': alice's profile is `ODFC_alice.vhdx`, a 30 GB virtual disk, and step 5 says zeros would hand Windows a corrupt disk that looks valid. The rule that telling the three apart is the engine's job is RFC 0 §6.1. The slide's rule is §2's MUST.

placement.title: Where the bytes sit on disk
items: The journal appends to a few [[append-stream|streams]], and each stream takes the writes of many files at once. Every [[record|record]] goes at the end of its stream, so even a file written in order is stored out of order, interleaved with other files.
Nothing relates an [[extent|extent]]'s position in the file to its position on disk.
The [[journal|journal]] never writes into space freed inside a [[segment|segment]]. A write that fills a gap in a file goes wherever its stream has got to, like any other write.
There is one journal per disk, shared by every [[share|share]] placed on that disk. Each record carries the [[share-tag|tag]] of the share that wrote it.
placement.notes: §2 (a gap is a gap in the file, not in storage; the placement figure: 'a sequential file is stored out of order, interleaved with other files'), §1, §3 (tags). Few streams, many files: RFC 28 §2.2 (the number of append streams is configurable, 16 proposed; writes to different FileIDs may proceed concurrently).

quizGap.question: Nobody has ever written the first MiB of a file, and a client reads it. What does the [[journal]] answer?
options: Zeros for the whole MiB, since a never-written range reads as zeros.
An error saying the range is a hole that nobody ever wrote.
It lists the MiB as missing and leaves the caller's buffer untouched.
why: Only the metadata knows that a [[hole]] reads as zeros. The [[journal]] never returns zeros for bytes it does not hold, since they might be evicted or lost data.
The [[journal]] cannot tell a [[hole]] from bytes that were [[evict|evicted]] or [[lost]], because all three look the same to it. Telling them apart is the [[engine]]'s job.
The [[journal]] reports every range it does not hold as [[missing]], whatever the cause. The [[engine]] then learns from the metadata that this one is a hole.
quizGap.notes: §2: the gaps carry no explanation, and the journal MUST report a never-written, an evicted and a lost extent identically. §3.2 ReadAt: it MUST NOT zero-fill or short-read, missing is exact, and the buffer is left untouched. The caller distinguishes hole from eviction from loss (RFC 0 §6.1).

life.title: From a write to free space
life.notes: §3.1 Write, §3.3 Offload ('Offload makes content evictable; Release evicts it'), §3.5 Release, §7.1 Releasing storage, §7.2 Repack. A segment left with nothing live is retired by the journal on its own, without waiting for repack (§7.1).

offer.title: An [[offer|offer]] is frozen
items: `Offload` hands the offer to a callback from the engine. While the callback runs, the offer returns the bytes as they were when offered, even if a client overwrites them, because the [[carver|carver]] hashes them and the uploader reads them again later.
The engine calls `report` once for each [[block|block]] it commits, and the journal marks that block's [[extent|extents]] as offloaded at once.
If the callback returns an error, nothing is taken back. Extents already [[report|reported]] stay marked, and the others stay [[dirty|dirty]].
Reporting an extent that was never part of the offer is an error, and the journal rejects it.
bounds: The engine passes each call a size limit, and one offer never holds more dirty bytes than that.

Every [[segment|segment]] an offer reads is pinned: [[repack]] can neither move nor free it until the engine's callback returns. An offer stops adding extents at 64 pinned segments, or at 256 across all offers, though its first extent always fits. The rest waits for a later offer.
Every byte is checked against its [[record|record]]'s checksum before it is handed out.
offer.example: For example, one pass offers 64 MiB, which the engine carves into 16 blocks of 4 MiB. Block 3 commits first, and its 4 MiB can be evicted at once. Then block 9 fails, and everything reported before that stays marked.
offer.notes: §3.3 Offload: what an offer is, report block by block, 'limit bounds the dirty bytes one call offers' (the engine chooses it, RFC 8 §6.2), 'An offer pins a bounded number of segments' (every segment holding an offered record stays on disk, unmoved, until fn returns; repack cannot retire it meanwhile, §7.2), 'Offered returns no unverified byte'. The 64 and 256 bounds carry a decision marker: constants, not measured. They are 'proposals' in §3.3 and §10 question 4. When the next extent would pass a cap, the offer stops adding extents and offers the rest in a later call; the first extent always fits, so an offer is never empty (§3.3). Pinned segments are therefore bounded by the journal-wide bound plus one per running offer (§3.3).

repack.title: Space comes back in whole [[segment|segments]]
repack.ponytail: Freeing space a whole segment at a time means copying the live [[record|records]] that share the segment. When a segment is 85% live, about 5.7 bytes are copied for every byte freed. That cost has not been measured yet.
repack.notes: §3.5 (a release returns no storage), §7.1 (storage is freed in whole segments only; the ponytail marker with u ÷ (1 − u)), §7.2 Repack (selection: least live payload first; content preservation). The 20% in the scene is an illustration. The 'not measured' cost is benchmark J8 (§10 question 1). The spare: §7.1 (a segment's storage returns to the filesystem when unlinked, or to the spare pool when recycled as a spare) and §6 (a spare becomes a stream's next segment).

versions.title: Two numbers on every [[record|record]]
table: which bytes these are, and which is newer
the file, wherever it is held
a new one, assigned by the journal
the version the metadata recorded with the copy in the bucket
versions.footer: For every byte of a file, the newest content version the journal has applied is the one a read gets. A read never uses sequence numbers to choose its bytes. It only checks that the record it finds carries the number the journal expects. Sequence numbers order records during recovery. When bytes are uploaded, the metadata that records them keeps their content version, so bytes fetched back from the bucket come with the version they had.
versions.notes: §4.3 Versions (the table, abridged), §2 (the newest version applied wins), §4 (a lookup must be unambiguous without sequence numbers). Versions are assigned inside the file's serialised append (§3.1). Fill's version: §3.4, 'v is the content version of the ref the bytes were fetched from: its newest (RFC 6 §2.1)'; the filled record carries it. A read and sequence numbers: §4, 'The entry carries its record's sequence number only so a read can compare it with the header it finds and so a record that does not verify can be named'. The repack row is §4.3's 'a repack copy of content'; a header-only record that repack carries forward keeps both its numbers (§4.3, §7.2), which the slide leaves out.

fill.title: A fetch races a new write
fill.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios', the fetch that races a write; §3.2 (asOf), §3.4 Fill: Fill(ctx, id, off, p, asOf, v), where asOf is the change version ReadAt returned (the check) and v the content version of the ref the bytes came from (stamped on the record). Outcome: the old bucket bytes never land over the new write, and are never marked offloaded. The check is deliberately coarse: a needless refusal costs only a cache miss.

floor.title: A file the journal holds nothing of
items: When a file is deleted, or everything it held is released, the journal stops tracking it and keeps no change version for it.

A [[fill]] for such a file is checked instead against one of 4,096 [[floor-bucket|floor buckets]], picked by a hash of the file's ID. When the journal stops tracking a file, it raises the file's bucket to the file's last change version, so an older fill is still refused.

The table has a fixed size, so it does not grow with the number of files the journal once held. The cost is that a change to one file can refuse fills of the other files in its bucket, about one file in 4,096. Such a needless refusal costs only a cache miss.
floor.notes: §3.4 Fill, floor buckets: 'The per-file change version is bounded by floor buckets: a fixed table of 4,096 versions, indexed by a hash of the FileID'; a file's entry is dropped when it holds no extent and no removal marker (after a Delete, or once everything it held was released), and dropping it raises the file's bucket to the entry's version; a file with no entry is compared against its bucket; at open every bucket starts at the highest content version on disk or in the floor, whichever is higher. Share raises every bucket to its floor before it returns the handle (§3, §3.4), so attaching a share can needlessly refuse the fills in flight of every file with no entry; attaches are rare, and such a refusal costs a cache miss. The decision marker: one bucket confines a delete's needless refusals to about one file in 4,096; 'a needless refusal costs only a cache miss'.

fillwrite.title: [[fill|Fill]] is not a write
table: the one recorded with the copy fetched
unset, so it still has to be offloaded
set, because it is offloaded already
fillwrite.footer: The two can share the code that appends records, but they are never one entry point with a parameter choosing between them. A wrong value would discard a client's write, or make content that is in no bucket evictable, and nothing would fail at the time.
fillwrite.notes: §3.4 Fill, and its subsection 'Fill is not a write'. Fill is as safety-critical as Release: bytes passed to it become content the journal will release. The RFC's words: an implementation SHOULD share their append machinery and MUST NOT expose them as one entry point selected by a parameter.

quizFill.question: A read finds a range [[missing]] at v50. Before the fetch returns, a client writes 4 KiB into it. What does `Fill` do?
options: It writes nothing and returns an error, because the file has changed.
It writes the fetched bytes only where the new 4 KiB did not land.
It writes the whole range, putting the bucket's bytes over the new 4 KiB.
why: The write raised the file's [[change-version|change version]] to v51, newer than the v50 the read returned. So `Fill` writes none of the fetched bytes.
A [[fill]] does leave held bytes alone, but a file that changed after the read gets no fill at all. Not even the bytes around the new 4 KiB are written.
A [[fill]] never overwrites bytes the [[journal]] holds. Putting the bucket's older bytes over the new write would lose the client's data.
quizFill.notes: §3.4 Fill: 'A Fill older than the file is refused': if the file's change version is newer than asOf, Fill writes nothing and returns a distinct error (a MUST in the RFC); Fill never overwrites any part of a held extent (a MUST NOT). 'Start here · Scenarios', the fetch that races a write.

survive.title: What survives what
survive.c1: A [[record|record]] that was written survives, because the operating system still holds it. `WriteAt` writes the record before it returns.
survive.c2: A record that was not yet synced does not survive the loss of the host. A client that never flushes can lose at most the writes it made within one time bound before the failure.
survive.c3Title: After a flush or the time bound
survive.c3: Synced records survive a host crash and a power loss. One sync serves every writer waiting on the same stream.
survive.footer: No setting can declare a [[journal|journal]] not [[durable|durable]]. At restart, a half-written record at the end of a stream's newest segment is cut off as a torn tail, and is not reported as damage. A record that was already synced is never cut off this way: if it is damaged, the damage is reported.
survive.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios' (the power fails half a second after a write nobody flushed); §5.1 ordering rules; §5.2 Syncing (sync bound, group commit, 'no setting declares a journal not durable'); RFC 28 §3.3 (torn tail). RFC 28 §3.3: a torn tail exists only in the newest segment of a stream, the only one that could have been open for append at a crash; damage to records proven synced, by a later record's synced-through offset or by a sync mark the engine recorded, is corruption and is reported, never cut off as a torn tail.

failedsync.title: A failed [[sync|sync]] is not a slow one
failedsync.lead: After a failed sync the OS may have dropped the pages it could not write and marked them clean, so a later sync can “succeed” without writing them.
steps: Everything written to the [[segment|segment]] since its last successful sync, which the RFC calls the window, counts as not [[durable|durable]].
When a segment is full, the journal seals it by appending a seal marker at its end. A failed segment gets nothing more appended, not even that marker, and the stream carries on in a new segment.

The [[journal|journal]] appends the window's [[record|records]] again in the new segment, taking them from its own copy in memory or reading them back and checking them against the checksum it kept. Otherwise it fails them as [[loss-event|loss events]].

If it fails them, the next `Sync` for each file that had a write in the window returns the error, and only that one. `Sync` is the call the engine makes when a client flushes a file. The [[write-verifier]] also changes, so that clients send their writes again.
failedsync.rule: A later successful sync never counts as success for writes made before the failure.
failedsync.notes: §5.3 A failed sync (no further append, 'not even a seal marker'); §5.1 (the last two ordering rules); §5.2 (the stream makes a segment durable when it rolls, because the seal marker must be durable before a successor exists; 'The journal's part in a client's flush is Sync'); §3.1 (Sync names files); 'Start here · Scenarios' (the disk reports an error). The 'only that one' is the conformance check of §5.3 'a failed window is reported once': the next Sync(F) fails, the one after succeeds. Header-only records are always re-appended, never failed, outside a read-only journal.

readonly.title: When the disk stops taking writes
readonly.lead: The [[journal|journal]] turns **read-only** until it is closed and reopened if a call gets `EROFS`, or if the new [[segment|segment]] a stream moved to after a failure also fails before any [[sync|sync]] in it has succeeded.
items: Reads go on, and every [[held-extent|held extent]] is served, [[dirty|dirty]] ones included.
Every call that would append a [[record|record]] fails at once with `ErrJournalReadOnly`.
Every record not yet synced, on every stream, is failed in the same way as a failed window.
When the journal is reopened, its recovery decides which records are [[durable|durable]].
readonly.notes: §5.4 A journal that cannot write. One exception to the second item: DropOlder, which still drops in memory (§3.3). Without the rule, a filesystem refusing every write would drain the spares and the headroom one failed call at a time.

capacity.title: A full [[journal|journal]] refuses at once
items: Before it accepts a write's bytes, the journal reserves space for them against the [[share]]'s limit and against the journal's maximum size.
If they do not fit, `WriteAt` fails **at once** with `ErrNoSpace`, which names the limit that was hit. It does no I/O and does not wait.
It does not wait because only the [[engine]]'s own calls free space. A journal that waited would be waiting for its own caller.

While [[offload|offload]], [[release|release]] and [[repack|repack]] can still free space, the engine answers [[retry-later]] instead of an error. An NFS client then sends the write again, and an SMB request is kept pending.
capacity.headroom: [[record|Records]] that free space, such as releases, truncates, deletes and seals, draw on a reserved [[headroom]] outside every limit, so a full journal can still release. Once less than half of the headroom is left, content writes are refused first.
capacity.notes: §6 Capacity: the two bounds, 'a refusal is immediate, and named', records without bytes, the headroom and its half rule. Checking a counter and then deciding is not conformant: the reservation must be atomic. RFC 8 §10.2 holds the engine's table of answers.

limits.title: The six limits a write can hit
items: **Share** and **journal**: each [[share]] has a limit on the bytes of its records, and the journal has a maximum size on disk, counted in whole [[segment|segments]].
**Index**: a configured cap on how many [[extent|extents]] the [[placement-index|placement index]] may hold in memory.
**Headroom**: once less than half of the [[headroom]] is left, content writes are refused, so that the records that free space can still be appended.

**Version limit**: a client can see a [[content-version|content version]] before its record is synced, so after a crash the journal must never hand out that version again. It never gives out one at or above the [[version-limit|version limit]], which the engine records in the metadata store ahead of time. A write that would reach it is refused until the engine raises it.
**Spare pool**: when a [[append-stream|stream]]'s segment is full, the stream moves to an empty spare segment that the journal made in advance. If no spare is ready, the write is refused.
limits.footer: A refusal at the spare pool clears on its own once a new spare is ready, so the engine simply retries. Every other limit clears only once the engine frees space.
limits.notes: §6 Capacity: the two bounds (a share's limit on its record bytes, the journal's maximum on allocated storage in whole segments), 'a refusal is immediate, and named', the headroom's half rule, the spare pool ('When a stream's segment fills, a spare becomes its next segment and the journal makes a new spare off the write path'; a content write that needs a segment while no spare is ready is refused naming the spare pool; 'spare clears on its own and is retried, every other limit clears only once the engine reclaims space'). §4.2 (ExtentLimit, the index entry bound). §4.3 (the version limit: no version issued at or above it, raised by the caller ahead by time; a write that would reach it fails with ErrNoSpace naming the limit, answered ErrDelay until the raise commits, RFC 8 §2.7 and §10.2).

full.title: A large copy meets a full [[journal|journal]]
steps: A write needs more space than the journal's maximum allows, so `WriteAt` fails at once with `ErrNoSpace`.

The [[engine|engine]] does not fail the write. It frees space and then tries the write again itself. If that takes a while, the client is told [[retry-later|retry-later]] (`ErrDelay`) rather than an error: an NFS client sends the write again, and an SMB request is kept pending.
The engine releases [[extent|extents]] that were already reported [[offload|offloaded]]. The [[release|release]] records it appends draw on the [[headroom|headroom]].
A release frees no disk space by itself. [[repack|Repack]] then copies a [[segment|segment]]'s live records forward and unlinks the segment file.
The engine's retry comes within the client's deadline, and the write fits.
full.outcome: The limit is never overrun, and no [[dirty|dirty]] byte is dropped to make room.
full.notes: 'Start here · Scenarios', the journal is full while a large copy streams in (step 2: the engine answers retry-later; step 5: the engine retries within the client's deadline); §3.5, §6, §7.2. Who retries: RFC 8 §10.2 has the engine repack or evict and retry, answering ErrDelay while it is still refused; RFC 0's glossary row for retry-later and its 'journal at capacity' row: NFS answers NFS4ERR_DELAY / NFS3ERR_JUKEBOX and the client retries, SMB holds the request pending with an interim response.

quizSync.question: A [[sync]] of a [[segment]] fails with the I/O error `EIO`, then a second sync of it succeeds. What of the writes the failed sync should have covered?
options: The second sync covers them, so from then on they count as durable.
They are appended again in a new segment, or failed as loss events.
The journal turns read-only, and its recovery decides which survived.
why: After a failed [[sync]] the OS may have marked pages clean without writing them. So a later success proves nothing about writes made before the failure.
Those writes count as not [[durable]]. The [[journal]] appends their [[record|records]] again in a new [[segment]], or fails them as [[loss-event|loss events]].
A sync that fails with `EIO` only moves the stream to a new [[segment]]. The [[journal]] turns read-only on `EROFS`, or when that new segment fails too before a sync succeeds in it.
quizSync.notes: §5.3 A failed sync: everything written since the segment's last successful sync is not durable, and the window is re-appended to the new segment or failed as loss events (unless the journal has turned read-only). §5.1: a failed sync never satisfies (MUST NOT), by a later success, a Sync for writes made before the failure. §5.4: read-only on EROFS, or when the spare a stream moved to also fails before any sync in it has succeeded. The question names EIO so that §5.4's read-only transition, which an EROFS would trigger, does not apply.

index.title: Two indexes, easy to confuse
table: every [[record|record]] of that segment, live or not
index.footer: During recovery, the [[placement-index]] is rebuilt from the catalogs, or by reading the segments themselves where there is no catalog, as in a segment that was never sealed. For each file it is a set ordered by start offset, such as a B-tree, so that looking up one offset costs O(log n). Walking the extents one by one is forbidden.
index.notes: §4 (the comparison table, abridged: the catalog lives inside each sealed segment, describes every record live or superseded, is immutable for the life of its segment and is not authoritative; the index is built from the catalogs or a scan at recovery, never the other way round; an active segment has no catalog until it seals), §4.1 (the required bounds), 'Representation' (B-tree is a SHOULD). The catalog's layout is RFC 28 §2.4.
index.catalog: When a [[segment]] is sealed, the journal writes a catalog inside it that lists every [[record]] the segment holds. The catalog never changes afterwards, so it still lists records that are no longer live, because a later write replaced them or a release dropped them. That is why only the placement index is authoritative.

indexsize.title: The index grows with [[extent|extents]], not bytes
table: Index, extents written in offset order
Index, extents written in random order
indexsize.footer: Extents written in random order leave the index's B-tree nodes less full, so an entry costs about 69 bytes instead of 53. Past a configured bound (`ExtentLimit`), writes and [[fill|fills]] are refused with an error that names the index, so the journal never degrades silently. Removals and [[release|releases]] are not refused at the bound itself, so the count can come down again.
indexsize.notes: §4.2: about 53 bytes an entry in order and 69 in random order, measured in one file of 10^6 extents; many small files cost more per entry. Releases, deallocates and clone targets that split an extent are refused once the count is an eighth above the bound; reports, truncates, deletes and Forget never are.

numbers.w1: the size of one [[segment|segment]], as proposed in the RFC's examples
numbers.w2: the proposed [[sync|sync]] bound, which is the most a client that never flushes can lose
numbers.w3: per index entry, so 1 TiB written in 64 KiB pieces needs about 0.9–1.2 GB of index
numbers.w4: the proposed caps on [[segment|segments]] pinned by one [[offer|offer]], and by all offers together
numbers.w5: records with no bytes after their header, such as releases and removals, that the proposed [[headroom|headroom]] can hold, about 14 MiB
numbers.w6: [[floor-bucket|floor buckets]], against which a [[fill|fill]] is checked when the journal holds nothing of its file
numbers.notes: 256 MiB: 'Start here · The problem' and §7.4. 1 s: §5.2 and 'Start here'. 53–69: §4.2. 64 and 256: §3.3. 65,536 and 14 MiB: §6 (journal.headroom_records). 4,096: §3.4. §10 question 4 says the headroom, reserves and pin bounds are unmeasured. The 256 MiB segment, the 1 s bound, the 64 · 256 pin bounds and the 65,536 headroom records are all proposals. Header-only records: §6 (releases, truncates, deletes and other records without bytes draw on the headroom).

shares.title: One [[journal|journal]], many [[share|shares]]
items: Each share works through its own journal `Handle`, which is the share's access to the journal, not a client's file handle. The share's [[share-tag|tag]] is written into every [[record|record]] it appends.
A tag names exactly one share. It is taken from a counter that never goes down, so a tag is never reused.
A call on a file that belongs to another tag is refused with `ErrOtherShare`. One share's bytes are never served through another share's journal `Handle`.
Each share has a limit, so that one share cannot take the whole disk. The limits of all the shares may add up to more than the journal's maximum.
shares.notes: §3 Interface: 'A tag names one share, once', 'A file is its share's, and the journal checks it'. §6: share limits. The journal Handle is §3's (*Journal).Share result, one share's access to the journal; the deck does not link the glossary's 'handle', which is a client's file handle. In a correct installation ErrOtherShare never fires; it guards against a clone, restore or move that skipped a step.

stranded.title: A [[share-tag|tag]] that no share claims
items: A tag can be left without a share when its [[share]] is deleted, or when the installation's metadata is restored from a backup. A restore creates each share afresh with a new tag, so the journal never serves bytes it held under the old tag as if they were the restored share's current content.
Before the node serves clients, the engine strands each such tag. From then on its bytes are never served through another share, nor [[evict|evicted]] or [[offer|offered]].

Once the node is serving, the engine exports the tag's bytes for **salvage**: it copies every byte the journal holds for the tag into files in a separate salvage directory, where an operator can recover them.

The export waits until serving has started so that it does not keep the node offline for hours. Only after it succeeds is the tag forgotten, because its bytes may be the only copy of a lost share's content.
stranded.notes: §3 Interface: 'A tag no share claims is stranded before serving and salvaged after' (a recovery import, which gives the shares new identities, or a share's deletion; Strand before serving; export of every held extent under salvage.path after serving starts, then Forget), the decision marker 'salvage runs after serving, not before' (exporting first would hold the installation offline for hours), 'A share attached as an import holds none of its old extents' (an import gets a new tag), and 'The journal offers no shortcut: a tag forgotten unread would drop dirty bytes that may be the only copy'. The caller's side is RFC 8 §2.5 step 5 and RFC 26 §2.3. An export of an encrypting share is sealed with a salvage data key; a failed export is a health condition, retried, and the tag stays stranded until it succeeds. Why a restore gets a new tag: §3, 'A share attached as an import holds none of its old extents' (an import gets a new tag, so calls on the old tag's files through it are refused and the share never serves stale, clean extents over what was written since).

concurrency.title: What must not block what
items: A read of one file never waits on a write to another file, on a [[sync|sync]], or on reclaiming a [[segment|segment]] it does not read.
A write waits only for its own file's append and for capacity.
A truncate, deallocate or delete never waits for an [[offload|offload]] pass to finish. The pass keeps the bytes it was offered.
Content versions are assigned while the file's appends run one at a time, so one file's versions are appended in the order they were assigned.
concurrency.notes: §8.1 What must not block what; §3.1 (version assignment). 'Waits for capacity' is §8.1's wording; §6 says a capacity refusal is immediate and never waits — the deck keeps both as the RFC words them.

testable.title: Testable on its own
items: A test opens a [[journal|journal]] on a temporary directory, drives its interface, and checks what comes back and what is on disk. No metadata store, [[carver|carver]], [[syncer|syncer]] or block store.
**The filesystem is real**, never faked, because torn tails and whether a write survived are properties of real storage.
**Storage loss is simulated beneath the journal.** A test layer remembers every unsynced write, and a simulated crash decides which of them survive.
**Time is virtual.** The [[sync|sync]] timer and every wait run on a clock that the test advances.
testable.kill: Killing the process proves nothing about durability. Unsynced writes stay in the operating system's page cache, so the test would prove a durability the journal does not have.
testable.notes: §1.3 It is testable on its own. §9.4 groups the checks: silent data loss, wedging and unbounded resource use, recovery, observability.

whom.title: Who needs to know what
whom.eng: The [[journal|journal]] decides no policy. You choose what to [[offload|offload]], when to [[release|release]], how much to [[repack|repack]], and how to answer each refusal. Pass to `Fill` only bytes fetched from the remote tier, or the journal will treat them as offloaded and may release content that exists nowhere else.
whom.ops: There is one journal per disk, sized by a maximum and by per-share limits. A full journal makes clients retry, not fail, while space can still be freed. Unclaimed tags are reported with their bytes and exported for salvage before they are forgotten.
whom.test: Tests use a real filesystem, a fault layer beneath the journal and virtual time. The checks look for silent data loss, for a journal that gets stuck or uses resources without bound, for recovery after a crash, and for what the journal reports about itself.
whom.notes: The deck's framing, from §3.4 (the caller of Fill), §3.5 and §7.2 (policy is the engine's), §6, §3 (strand and salvage), §1.3 and §9.4. The four groups are §9.4's: A silent data loss, B wedging and unbounded resource use, C recovery, D observability.

items: A read never fills with zeros or cuts short what it does not hold, and its `missing` list is exact.
`Release` refuses an [[extent|extent]] not reported [[offload|offloaded]], and a refused release frees nothing at all.
`Fill` never overwrites held bytes, and what it writes is marked offloaded.
The [[journal|journal]] marks exactly the reported extents, and never a newer write made over them.
A write reserves space before accepting bytes, and fails rather than go over a limit.
A later successful [[sync|sync]] never makes up for a failed one. A failed [[segment|segment]] is never appended to again.
rules.footer: The journal depends only on the standard library and the OS file interface, and an import test enforces that.
rules.notes: Each rule is a MUST or MUST NOT in the RFC: §3.2, §3.5, §3.4, §3.3, §3.1 and §6, §5.1 and §5.3; §1.1 for the import test.

nongoals.title: What the [[journal|journal]] never does
items: It never decides whether bytes it does not hold are a [[hole|hole]], [[evict|evicted]] or [[lost|lost]].
It never returns zeros for bytes it does not hold.
It knows nothing of what a [[chunk|chunk]] or a [[block|block]] is. A [[record|record]] is not a chunk.
It does not know which [[remote-tier|remote tier]] exists, and never speaks to one.
It imports no other component, such as the metadata store, the [[syncer|syncer]] or the [[carver|carver]].
nongoals.footer: Policy, such as what to [[evict|evict]] and when to [[repack|repack]], belongs to the [[engine]]. The journal supplies the mechanism.
nongoals.notes: §1.1 Non-goals (each a MUST NOT), §1.2. The footer: §3.5 ('the mechanism of eviction; the policy is the engine's') and §7.2 (the engine calls Repack with a budget and a scope).

questions: How much extra writing [[repack|repack]] causes under a load with many evictions has not been measured.
The index's memory use and lookup cost were measured, but the cost of inserting into it was not.

A [[sync|sync]] covers one [[append-stream|stream]], so when writers are spread over more streams, each sync serves fewer of them. In one measurement, a load that creates many files ran slower as streams were added. More streams also mean less waiting between writers, and which effect wins has not been measured.
The [[headroom|headroom]], the reserves and the pin bounds are proposals that have not been measured on a full [[journal|journal]].

[[repack|Repack]] cannot copy out of a [[segment|segment]] still being appended to, and a segment is sealed only when it is full or idle. The RFC still owes a rule that lets repack seal such a segment when space runs short.
The journal shows its space segment by segment, with each one's allocated and held bytes, but that per-segment breakdown does not yet show each segment's [[unreclaimed-bytes|unreclaimed bytes]].
openQuestions.notes: §10 Open questions (RFC 28 §5 holds the format's). Question 1 is benchmark J8. Question 3: more streams spread writers over more syncs; a create-heavy load measured slower as streams were added, unmeasured against the contention more streams remove. Question 5: a pass scoped to a share seals such a segment itself (a rule owed in Repack's contract, §7.2), so repack can reach its unreclaimed bytes. Question 6: the per-segment accounting of §4.4 (inspection) reports allocated and held bytes only. Repack and active segments: question 5 and RFC 8 §10.2 step 4 (each active segment holding the scope's unreclaimed bytes must be sealed so repack can reach them; a segment seals only when full or idle, RFC 28 §3.1).

steps: **09:00** — alice-pc writes 64 KiB at offset 2 GiB of a file. The journal appends them as **v41**, and the write is acknowledged.
**09:01** — The engine takes an **[[offer|offer]]** of v41, a frozen view of those bytes, and uploads a [[block|block]] holding them to the bucket `dfs-data`.
During the upload, alice-pc overwrites the same 64 KiB. The journal now serves **v42**, while the offer still reads v41.

The block commits and the engine **[[report|reports]]** the [[extent|extent]]. If the journal marked it by position in the file, v42 would look [[offload|offloaded]], and [[evict|eviction]] could drop the only copy of v42.
With RFC 1, the journal marks only the bytes it offered. v42 stays [[dirty|dirty]] and goes into the next offer.
A write of 8 KiB at offset 0 gets version 7, and the journal now holds the [[extent]] (0, 8K).
A second write of 8 KiB at offset 4K gets version 8 and covers the upper half of the first one.
The file now holds two [[extent|extents]]: (0, 4K) at v7 and (4K, 8K) at v8. The old v7 bytes at 4K–8K are still in their [[record|record]] on disk, but a read of them gets v8.
**WriteAt** appends a [[record]]. The extent is now held and **dirty**, which means it is not in the bucket yet, so a release of it is refused.
**Offload** hands the engine a frozen [[offer]]. The engine carves the bytes into [[block|blocks]], uploads them and commits them.
Each committed block's **[[report|report]]** sets the [[offloaded-bit|offloaded bit]] of exactly the extents it names.
**Release**, the way the engine evicts, makes the journal stop holding offloaded extents. It frees no disk space, and the bytes become **unreclaimed**.
**[[repack|Repack]]** copies the [[segment|segment]]'s live [[record|records]] forward and unlinks it. Only now does the space return.
After many releases, most of segment `0041.seg` is **unreclaimed**. Most of its bytes back nothing, yet the whole file stays allocated.
**Repack** prefers the segments with the least live payload and copies their live records forward, versions and offloaded bits unchanged.
Once the copies are [[durable|durable]], `0041.seg` is unlinked, or kept as an empty spare that a stream can take later as its next segment. Only now does the space come back.
Windows reads the first MiB of a file, `[0, 1 MiB)`. The journal holds none of it, so it answers **missing**, together with the file's [[change-version|change version]], v50.
The engine starts fetching those bytes from the bucket `dfs-data`.
Meanwhile alice-pc writes 4 KiB at offset 0. It gets v51, and the file's change version rises to v51.

The fetch returns. The engine calls `Fill` with the bytes, the version recorded with their copy in the bucket, and v50, the change version the read returned. The file has changed since v50, so Fill writes nothing and returns a distinct error.
